extracted.intended_audience: fantasy novelists (especially novice or intermediate writers learning to use multiple POVs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and writing fantasy novels that use more than one point-of-view, including common mistakes to avoid and practical rules about voice, number of POVs, distribution, and purpose. Focused on narrative strategy rather than line-level prose rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view choice (first vs third)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most multiple-POV books in fantasy are written in third person; it's difficult to include multiple distinct first-person voices in a single book and do a good job of it. Romantasy is an exception where readers like to be in the minds of love interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be intentional about whether you use first or third. Prefer third person for multiple POVs unless you have a strong reason and skill to handle multiple first-person voices. Consider how the POV choice will impact overall story and reader access to characters' thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of POV characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking on too many points of view (characters) can become confusing and convoluted rather quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a small cast of POVs (recommendation: 2–4). Remember each POV requires full development — an arc, plot, and distinctive voice — so only add POVs you can sustain. Determine necessity: you don't have to show every piece of the story; omission can improve the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each POV must have its own arc/plot/voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each point of view has a character that will have their own arc, plot, and voice separate from one another; writing multiple POVs is similar to writing a few novellas and mashing them together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan distinct arcs and plots for each POV and ensure each voice feels like a separate narrative. New writers should gain experience with single-POV stories before attempting multiple-POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid side-by-side identical stories (provide separate stakes/motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's hard to write many points of view if they're all experiencing the same events at the same times without their own stories happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each POV a reason to exist by creating different motives and storylines. Characters can share locations or events, but their goals and perspectives should create distinct narratives. The most compelling multiple-POV stories often have separate settings/stories that later converge (Game of Thrones as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness of character voice and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A huge mistake is making all characters act (and sound) the same — essentially one character with different names. A reader should be able to determine which viewpoint it is by reading just one paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters fully rounded with different world beliefs, actions, and decision-making styles. Use differences in thought processes, reactions, diction, and priorities so each POV reads as a unique person (example contrast: Jon Snow vs Daenerys vs Cersei). Chapter labels can help but should not be required for recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only include necessary viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every character gets a viewpoint. Adding a POV for a favorite side character often isn't necessary and will usually make the book confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the information shown can be conveyed another way before giving a character a POV. Avoid adding POVs purely to increase complexity; each POV must justify its presence in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality — don’t use multiple-POV as a trend
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers include multiple POVs because it's popular, but sometimes a story doesn't need more than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple-POV as a deliberate narrative device when it serves the plot or theme, not as a gimmick for marketing. Ensure the multiple perspectives are necessary to tell the story you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible (uneven) POV distribution dictated by story needs
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no rules for how many chapters each main character should get; forcing an every-other-chapter structure can produce pointless scenes and overly long books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the story dictate which POV appears and when. Uneven distribution can create momentum and curiosity about characters who haven't appeared recently; avoid mechanical, evenly split chapter assignment.
